metadata.file_name: 203. Kişman et al. (2026). Analysis of the Effects of World Bank Macroeconomic and Management Indicators on Sustainable Education Quality on PISA Scores Using the SHAP Explainable Artificial Intelligence Method.pdf
metadata.title: Analysis of the Effects of World Bank Macroeconomic and Management Indicators on Sustainable Education Quality on PISA Scores Using the SHAP Explainable Artificial Intelligence Method

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study constructs country-level datasets by combining PISA domain scores (PISAM, PISAR, PISAS) with World Bank governance/economic indicators, Economist Intelligence Unit democracy, and regional category dummies. The analytic sample is therefore an aggregate country/region-level modeling dataset rather than a student microdata file, and the manuscript does not report the use of PISA complex survey weights or replicate-weight procedures. Because the models are tree-based classifiers (Random Forest and XGBoost) trained on tabular country-level predictors, the paper does not specify any survey-weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) being applied. Data preparation includes missing-value checks with trend-based interpolation for PISA scores and scaling of numerical variables, followed by two-stage feature elimination (correlation thresholding and VIF-based multicollinearity reduction) before model training.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are country-level PISA domain scale means (PISAM, PISAR, PISAS) that are used to create Low/Medium/High achievement classes via fixed score thresholds. Plausible Values are typically generated for student-level cognitive achievement scales in PISA microdata; here the study uses aggregated domain means, so PV handling is not applicable to the modeled outcome. Missing-data handling is only partially described (PISA scores imputed via trend-based interpolation), but the paper does not provide a complete, explicit missing-data strategy for all predictors and for the final analytic dataset, representing a reporting gap.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The manuscript describes creating three separate country-level datasets (one per target: PISAM, PISAR, PISAS) using the same explanatory features (governance, economic capacity, democracy, regional category, and a centered observation year). It reports checking missing values and imputing unavailable PISA scores using trend-based interpolation across years, scaling numerical variables, and then applying two-stage feature selection (greedy correlation elimination with |r|≥0.90 followed by iterative VIF elimination with VIF>7.0). No explicit inclusion/exclusion rules for specific countries, years, or a final country count are reported in the provided text.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA Mathematics (PISAM) country-level domain means (Low/Medium/High classes)
main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost (best model): Class-based Precision/Recall/F1 — Low: 0.97/0.97/0.97 (Support 110); Medium: 0.91/0.93/0.92 (Support 107); High: 0.96/0.94/0.95 (Support 111). General metrics reported as Train Accuracy=1.0 and Test Accuracy=0.93–0.95; ROC-AUC reported in 0.98–1.00 band; Macro Avg and Weighted Avg ≈0.93–0.95.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA Mathematics (PISAM) country-level domain means the study leveraged Voice and Accountability, Control of Corruption, Political Stability, Regional Category, and GDP per capita to predict PISAM achievement class (Low/Medium/High), finding that governance indicators form the most salient institutional core and that class separation is further shaped by political stability and regional location. This indicates that strengthening accountability/anti-corruption capacity and stabilizing political institutions may be key levers for moving countries toward higher mathematics achievement profiles, though the results are predictive associations rather than causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA Reading (PISAR) country-level domain means (Low/Medium/High classes)
main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost (best model): Class-based Precision/Recall/F1 — Low: 0.95/0.97/0.96 (Support 108); Medium: 0.94/0.84/0.89 (Support 112); High: 0.90/0.97/0.93 (Support 108). General metrics reported as Train Accuracy=1.0 and Test Accuracy=0.93–0.95; ROC-AUC reported in 0.98–1.00 band; Macro Avg and Weighted Avg ≈0.93–0.95.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA Reading (PISAR) country-level domain means the study leveraged Voice and Accountability, Control of Corruption, GDP, GDP per capita, and Regional Category to predict PISAR achievement class (Low/Medium/High), finding that the model integrates economic capacity more explicitly into the governance-centered institutional core for reading outcomes. This indicates that education sustainability strategies for reading may require pairing governance reforms with targeted investments that expand economic capacity, while recognizing that SHAP-based explanations reflect model reliance rather than causal impact.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA Science (PISAS) country-level domain means (Low/Medium/High classes)
main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost (best model): Class-based Precision/Recall/F1 — Low: 0.95/1.00/0.97 (Support 107); Medium: 0.95/0.90/0.92 (Support 116); High: 0.94/0.95/0.95 (Support 105). General metrics reported as Train Accuracy=1.0 and Test Accuracy=0.93–0.95; ROC-AUC reported in 0.98–1.00 band; Macro Avg and Weighted Avg ≈0.93–0.95.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA Science (PISAS) country-level domain means the study leveraged Voice and Accountability, Control of Corruption, Political Stability, Regional Category, and GDP to predict PISAS achievement class (Low/Medium/High), finding that governance signals work together with regional bloc differentiation to distinguish higher science profiles. This indicates that science-focused sustainable education policy may benefit from regional benchmarking and institutional diffusion mechanisms alongside governance and stability improvements, while noting that the framework provides predictive/explanatory signals rather than causal prescriptions.

data.outcome_summary: The study builds three multi-class country-level classification models for PISA Mathematics (PISAM), Reading (PISAR), and Science (PISAS) by mapping each country’s domain mean into Low/Medium/High classes using fixed score thresholds. After imputing missing PISA scores via trend-based interpolation and scaling predictors, the authors apply two-stage feature selection (correlation elimination with |r|≥0.90 and VIF elimination with VIF>7.0) to reduce multicollinearity. Random Forest and XGBoost are trained separately for each target, with XGBoost selected as best-performing; class-wise Precision/Recall/F1 are mostly above 0.90, and general performance is reported as Train Accuracy=1.0, Test Accuracy=0.93–0.95, and ROC-AUC in the 0.98–1.00 range. Explanations are produced with SHAP and evaluated using Fidelity and Faithfulness (PISAM 0.95/0.85; PISAR 0.89/0.92; PISAS 0.89/0.89), supporting explanation reliability. Limitations include the use of aggregate country-level indicators (no within-country heterogeneity) and the fact that SHAP-based attributions are predictive associations, not causal effects.
